nameStory: This tiny freshwater creature gets its name from the Greek words 'macro' meaning large and 'cyclops' referring to the mythical one-eyed giant. Like its legendary namesake, this copepod has a single prominent eye in the center of its head, though 'large' is definitely relative when you're talking about something smaller than a pinhead!
description: The dusky copepod is a microscopic freshwater crustacean that lives in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These tiny animals look like miniature shrimp with a teardrop-shaped body and long, feathery antennae that they use like oars to paddle through the water. At just 1-2 millimeters long, they're barely visible to the naked eye as tiny specks darting through the water. Despite their small size, they're actually related to lobsters and crabs!

idTips.label: Single red eye
idTips.description: Look for a bright red or orange dot in the center of the head area - this is the distinctive cyclops eye that gives them their name

idTips.label: Jerky swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves through water with characteristic stop-and-go bursts, unlike the smooth gliding of other tiny water creatures

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: Two prominent, branched antennae extend from the front like tiny feathers, constantly beating to propel them forward

idTips.label: Brownish coloration
idTips.description: Body appears dusky brown or grayish when viewed under magnification, darker than many other copepods

idTips.label: Egg sacs
idTips.description: Females carry two oval egg sacs attached to either side of their body like tiny balloons

habitat: Found in the shallow, weedy areas of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams where organic matter accumulates. They prefer areas with plenty of decaying plant material and algae, often congregating near the bottom or among aquatic vegetation. You'll find them in both temporary pools and permanent water bodies throughout New England's lowlands and valleys.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, with populations growing rapidly. Egg-carrying females become common as reproduction kicks into high gear.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when they're easiest to spot. Look for them in shallow, sun-warmed areas of ponds and lakes.
seasonality.fall: Numbers begin to decline but they remain active until water temperatures drop significantly. Some individuals prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Many survive under ice in a dormant state, though some populations may continue limited activity in deeper, warmer water.

funFact: A single female dusky copepod can produce over 1,000 offspring in her lifetime, and her babies can start reproducing when they're only two weeks old - meaning a single individual could theoretically have over a million descendants in just one summer!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other copepods, but the dusky brown color and single red eye are diagnostic. Water fleas (Daphnia) are similar-sized but have two large compound eyes and a more rounded body shape. Remember: one eye means cyclops, two eyes means water flea.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'copepods' (meaning 'oar feet'), they actually swim primarily with their antennae, not their feet. The feet are mainly used for grasping food and surfaces. Many people are surprised to learn these microscopic creatures are actually crustaceans - the same group that includes lobsters and crabs.
compareHints: The dusky copepod is darker and slightly larger than its close relative, the white copepod (Macrocyclops albidus), which appears more translucent or pale. Both share the characteristic single red eye, but the dusky copepod's brownish coloration makes it easier to spot against light backgrounds. The white copepod tends to prefer cleaner, less organic-rich waters than its dusky cousin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White copepods can be distinguished from their close relative, the brownish copepod (Macrocyclops fuscus), primarily by their pale, translucent coloration versus the darker brownish tint of their cousin.
